message.content:
The “color” of the sea isn’t fixed—it’s a mix of many factors:

| Factor | How it changes the appearance |
|--------|------------------------------|
| **Depth** | Shallow waters look turquoise or greenish‑blue because they reflect more sunlight; deep oceans appear darker blue or even black at great depths. |
| **Water Clarity / Turbidity** | Clear water lets light penetrate deeper, giving a vivid azure hue. Murky or algae‑rich water appears greener or brownish due to suspended particles scattering light. |
| **Sun Angle & Time of Day** | Early morning or late afternoon rays give warm golden or pink tints; midday sun produces bright cyan or teal shades. |
| **Surface Conditions** | Calm surfaces show crisp colors; waves scatter light, making the surface seem lighter or milky. |
| **Underlying Bottom** | Light-colored sand or coral reefs beneath shallow water can tint the overlying water toward yellow or orange. |

So while we often think of the sea as “deep blue,” its actual color ranges from pale aqua near shorelines to dark indigo in abyssal zones—and everything in between depending on those conditions!
